name: Budhi Chanderi Ancient Forest Tirth
address: Budhi Chanderi Ancient Forest Tirth, Chanderi, District Ashoknagar, Madhya Pradesh - 473446
description: Budhi Chanderi Ancient Forest Tirth is an auspicious Digambar Jain pilgrimage destination situated in Chanderi, Madhya Pradesh. A dramatic ruined medieval temple city situated in dense forest approximately 15 km northwest of modern Chanderi. Contains the surviving remnants of over 20 stone Jain temples dating from the 10th to 12th centuries CE under the Gurjara-Pratiharas and Chandelas, celebrated in Chapter 13 of Dr. Kailash Chand Jain's treatise.
history: Budhi Chanderi was the original metropolis of the Chanderi region and one of the earliest prominent seats (pithas) of the Digambar Mula Sangha Kundakundanvaya. Scores of inscribed tirthankara pedestals and monolithic pillars bear dates ranging from Samvat 1050 to 1250. In the late medieval period, the population relocated to current Chanderi, leaving these sacred stone sanctuaries sheltered within the Vindhyan forests.
religious_significance: Venerated ancient Digambar Atishaya Kshetra documented in medieval Tirtha-Malas and Bhattaraka records.
moolnayak_details: Bhagwan Parshvanatha & Rishabhdeva, in contemplative Padmasana (Seated) posture, measuring approximately Colossal monolithic reliefs, sculpted from Buff Sandstone, dating to the 11th Century CE, (Multi-hooded serpent canopy, Yaksha Dharanendra, and Yakshi Padmavati carved in high relief.).

name: Chittorgarh Fort Jain Temples & Kirti Stambha (Tower of Fame)
hindi_name: चित्तौड़गढ़ दुर्ग दिगम्बर जैन मंदिर एवं कीर्ति स्तम्भ
address: Chittorgarh Fort Jain Temples & Kirti Stambha (Tower of Fame), Chittorgarh Fort, District Chittorgarh, Rajasthan - 312001
description: Chittorgarh Fort Jain Temples & Kirti Stambha (Tower of Fame) is an auspicious Digambar Jain pilgrimage destination situated in Chittorgarh Fort, Rajasthan. A monumentally significant fortified ensemble within Chittorgarh Fort featuring the world-famous 12th-century Kirti Stambha (Tower of Fame) and the 11th-century Satbis Deori (27 shrines) temple complex. The 22-meter-high, seven-storeyed Kirti Stambha was commissioned by the Digambar Jain merchant Jeevandhar (Jija Bhagerwala) under the spiritual guidance of Bhattaraka Dharmachandra, dedicated to Bhagwan Adinatha. Conserved by the Archaeological Survey of India and documented in GoI centenary records ('Archaeology in India', 1967).
history: Chittorgarh (ancient Chitrakoot) served as an eminent sanctuary and regional seat of Digambar Jain learning and monastic culture. In the late 12th century (c. 1190–1200 CE), merchant Jeevandhar, son of Solakh of the Bhagerwal community, commissioned the soaring Kirti Stambha to proclaim the glory of the Tirthankara dharma. The tower was completed by his son Punyasimha. In 1468 CE (VS 1525), following lightning damage, the monument was carefully repaired by local Jain guilds under Mewar royal patronage. The fort also houses the historic Satbis Deori complex containing 27 shrines. The Archaeological Survey of India has carried out structural stabilization and lightning arrestor installations on the tower.
religious_significance: Paramount monument of Digambar Jain architectural pride in Rajasthan and prominent UNESCO World Heritage Site landmark.
moolnayak_details: Bhagwan Adinatha (Rishabhadeva - Chaumukha & Colossal Carvings), in contemplative Kayotsarga (Standing) & Padmasana (Seated) posture, sculpted from Carved Local Sandstone, dating to the 12th Century CE, (Distinctive Digambar vitaraga features; 5-foot standing Adinatha figure prominently enshrined on the lower story.).

name: Dilwara Marble Jain Temple Complex (Mount Abu)
hindi_name: दिलवाड़ा संगमरमर जैन मंदिर समूह (माउंट आबू)
address: Dilwara Marble Jain Temple Complex (Mount Abu), Mount Abu, District Sirohi, Rajasthan - 307501
description: Dilwara Marble Jain Temple Complex (Mount Abu) is an auspicious Digambar Jain pilgrimage destination situated in Mount Abu, Rajasthan. A world-renowned pinnacle of medieval Indian marble temple architecture perched atop Mount Abu in Rajasthan. Built between the 11th and 13th centuries CE, the sacred complex comprises five monumental sanctuaries: Vimal Vasahi (consecrated 1031 CE by Dandapadati Vimala Shah to Lord Rishabhanatha), Luna Vasahi (consecrated 1230 CE by ministers Vastupala and Tejapala to Lord Neminatha), Pittalhar (Adinatha with massive brass colossus), Parshvanatha, and Mahavira Swami. Documented by the Archaeological Survey of India in 'Archaeology in India' (GoI 1967, p. 46) for its historic structural restoration and marble chemical conservation.
history: The Dilwara temples were established under the Chaulukya (Solanki) and Vaghela rulers of Gujarat. Vimal Vasahi was founded in 1031 CE by Vimala Shah, governor of Chandravati and commander of King Bhimadeva I, seeking spiritual expiation. Luna Vasahi was consecrated in 1230 CE by the eminent Porwad brothers Vastupala and Tejapala in memory of their brother Luniga, supervised by master architect Sobhandeva. During the 14th century, the temples suffered damage during regional campaigns but underwent meticulous restoration in 1321 CE by Lalla and Vijada. In the 20th century, the Archaeological Survey of India undertook specialized structural consolidation of the cantilevered marble domes, bracket lintels, and intricate hanging pendants (padmasila), as documented in ASI centenary reports.
religious_significance: One of the most sacred and artistically revered Jain Tirthas in western India, celebrated globally as the ultimate triumph of stone carving devotion.
moolnayak_details: Bhagwan Rishabhanatha (Vimal Vasahi) & Neminatha (Luna Vasahi), in contemplative Padmasana (Seated) posture, sculpted from Pure White Makrana Marble, dating to the 11th–13th Century CE, (Serene meditative posture seated on carved lion thrones, flanked by fly-whisk bearers and celestial vidyadharas.).

description: Gerusoppe (Nagire) Chaturmukha Basadi Complex is an auspicious Digambar Jain pilgrimage destination situated in Honnavar, Karnataka. The riverside royal capital of the medieval Saluva (Nagire) Jain dynasty on the banks of the Sharavathi River. Ruled in the 16th century by the legendary Jain Queen Chennabhairadevi (the 'Pepper Queen' who reigned for 54 years). Contains the exquisite grey granite Chaturmukha Basadi, documented in Chapter 13 of Dr. Kailash Chand Jain's treatise.
history: Flourished from the 14th to 17th centuries as a premier maritime trading and spiritual hub of Coastal Karnataka. Queen Chennabhairadevi gave asylum to Saraswat Brahmins and constructed monumental basadis, chhatris, and Nishidhi stones, maintaining sovereign independence against Portuguese naval expeditions.
religious_significance: Supreme historical monument of Coastal Karnataka Digambar Jain heritage.
moolnayak_details: Chaturmukha Tirthankaras (Adinatha, Shantinatha, Parshvanatha, Mahavira), in contemplative Padmasana (Seated) posture, measuring approximately 4 feet each, sculpted from Grey Granite, dating to the 16th Century CE, (Four serene identical granite icons facing east, west, north, and south in the garbhagriha.).

description: Hanumantal Bada Digambar Jain Mandir is an auspicious Digambar Jain pilgrimage destination situated in Jabalpur, Madhya Pradesh. Hanumantal Bada Jain Mandir is the paramount historic Digambar Jain temple complex of Jabalpur, situated serenely on the edge of Hanumantal lake. Originally erected in 1686 CE (Vikram Samvat 1743), it houses 22 distinct sanctums (vedis), making it the largest historic Jain temple complex in central India.
history: Erected in 1686 CE by the Jain community on the embankment of the historic Hanumantal water body, this vast fortress-like shrine preserves over 22 sanctums housing idols dating from the 10th century Kalachuri period to the Maratha and Bundela eras. It houses a celebrated ancient Shastra Bhandar (Grantha Bhandar) containing rare palm-leaf and paper illuminated manuscripts. Rabindranath Tagore stayed here in 1930 and immortalized its serene spiritual atmosphere in his memoirs.
religious_significance: Premier Atishaya Kshetra of Jabalpur and major center of Digambar Jain learning and manuscript preservation in Mahakoshal.
moolnayak_details: Bhagwan Adinatha (Rishabhanatha), in contemplative Padmasana (Seated) posture, measuring approximately 3.5 feet, sculpted from Black Touchstone (Kasauti Pashan), dating to the 10th–11th Century CE (Kalachuri Dynasty), (Exquisitely carved in deep black touchstone with cascading shoulder jatas, bull emblem (vrishabha) on pedestal, flanked by Gomukha Yaksha and Chakreshwari Devi.).

name: Kesariyaji Rishabhdeo Tirth (Dhulev)
address: Kesariyaji Rishabhdeo Tirth (Dhulev), Rishabhdeo (Dhulev), District Udaipur, Rajasthan - 313001
description: Kesariyaji Rishabhdeo Tirth (Dhulev) is an auspicious Digambar Jain pilgrimage destination situated in Rishabhdeo (Dhulev), Rajasthan. Magnificent ancient tirtha enshrining a 9th-century colossal black marble idol of Bhagwan Rishabhdev in Padmasana posture. Widely venerated for massive offerings of pure saffron (Kesar), earning the sanctuary the beloved title 'Kesariyaji'. The local indigenous Bhil community worships the idol with heartfelt devotion as 'Kalaji' or 'Kaliya Baba'. The temple has been subjected to administrative takeover by the Rajasthan State Devasthan Department, curtailing traditional Digambar autonomy and ritual prakshal.
history: The sanctuary boasts a rich epigraphical history dating from the 9th to the 17th centuries under the patronage of the Maharanas of Mewar. Mewar rulers preserved royal firmans ensuring customary Jain worship. Following the merger of princely states, the Rajasthan State Government assumed direct bureaucratic control under the Devasthan Department, prompting decades of constitutional litigation.
religious_significance: One of the most revered Atishaya Kshetras in Western India, sacred to Jains and revered by tribal communities.
moolnayak_details: Bhagwan Rishabhdev (Kesariyaji), in contemplative Padmasana (Seated) posture, sculpted from Polished Black Schist Stone, dating to the 9th Century CE, (Unclad Digambar Adinatha seated with Bull emblem and flowing hair locks (Jata).).

address: Mandavgadh (Mandu) Digambar Jain Bada Mandir & Atishaya Kshetra, Mandu, District Dhar, Madhya Pradesh - 454001
description: Mandavgadh (Mandu) Digambar Jain Bada Mandir & Atishaya Kshetra is an auspicious Digambar Jain pilgrimage destination situated in Mandu, Madhya Pradesh. A renowned medieval hill-fort pilgrimage sanctuary atop the Vindhyan plateau. Detailed in historical chronicles of Central India and archaeological surveys, Mandu (ancient Mandapadurga) was a vibrant center of Digambar Jain architecture, housing rare 10th- to 15th-century Kasauti stone and marble Digambar Tirthankara colossi.
history: Epigraphs confirm Digambar Jain shrines at Mandapadurga from the Paramara era (10th–13th centuries) through the Malwa Sultanate period. Pious Digambar Shravakas and merchant families commissioned grand stone temples, preserved sacred manuscripts in Shastra Bhandars, and hosted numerous Digambar Munis in the mountain retreats.
religious_significance: Revered Digambar Atishaya Kshetra dedicated to Lord Suparshvanatha, visited by centuries of pilgrimage caravans across Malwa.
moolnayak_details: Bhagwan Suparshvanatha, in contemplative Padmasana (Seated) posture, measuring approximately 3 feet, sculpted from White Marble & Kasauti Stone, dating to the 14th Century CE, (Seven-hooded serpent canopy and swastika symbol in pure Digambar meditative posture.).

name: Qutb Complex Ancient Jain Sanctuaries & Spolia (Quwwat-ul-Islam)
hindi_name: कुतुब परिसर प्राचीन जैन मंदिर अवशेष एवं दालान (कुव्वत-उल-इस्लाम)
address: Qutb Complex Ancient Jain Sanctuaries & Spolia (Quwwat-ul-Islam), Mehrauli, District South Delhi, Delhi - 470001
description: Qutb Complex Ancient Jain Sanctuaries & Spolia (Quwwat-ul-Islam) is an auspicious Digambar Jain pilgrimage destination situated in Mehrauli, Delhi. The foundational archaeological site of medieval Delhi within Lal Kot (Qila Rai Pithora). The colonnaded cloisters and courtyard surrounding the Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque were assembled from the architectural spolia of 27 dismantled pre-Islamic Hindu and Digambar Jain temples, explicitly recorded in the 1191–1193 CE Arabic gateway inscription. Detailed by 19th-century archaeologists Carr Stephen, Alexander Cunningham, and James Fergusson, the site preserves surviving Digambar iconography including carved Tirthankara panels, bell-and-chain pillar motifs, and corbelled lantern ceilings.
history: During the Tomara and Chauhan dynasties (10th–12th century CE), Lal Kot and surrounding Dhillika flourished as a major center of Digambar Jain culture, trade, and temple building. Following the conquest of Delhi by Qutb-ud-din Aibak in 1191–1192 CE (587 Hijri), materials from twenty-seven prominent temples within the citadel were dismantled and re-erected to construct the congregational mosque. Major-General Alexander Cunningham identified that the majority of the surviving ornate pillars belonged to Jain temples due to the distinctive rows of bells on chains, floral arabesques, and defaced Tirthankara reliefs on lintel brackets. Archaeological excavations conducted under J.D. Beglar in 1871 revealed the original pre-Islamic temple plinths and platforms directly beneath the mosque pavement.
religious_significance: Of monumental archaeological and epigraphical importance, serving as physical testimony to the flourishing Digambar Jain architectural landscape of pre-Sultanate Dhillika (Delhi).
moolnayak_details: Ancient Tomara-Chauhan Tirthankara Panels, in contemplative Padmasana (Seated) posture, sculpted from Carved Delhi Quartzite & Red Sandstone, dating to the 10th–12th Century CE, (Surviving relief carvings of seated Tirthankaras in Padmasana with attendants and Shrivatsa marks on roofing slabs, lintels, and pillar bases.).

description: One of North India's most prominent Atishay Kshetras, renowned for the miraculous appearance of the white stone idol of 8th Tirthankara Bhagwan Chandraprabhu during excavation in 1956.

description: A world-renowned Digambara Jain Atishay Kshetra dedicated to the 6th Tirthankara, Bhagwan Padmaprabhu, where a miraculous white marble idol was unearthed in May 1944.

name: Shri Digambar Jain Lal Mandir (Red Temple, Chandni Chowk)

address: Shri Digambar Jain Lal Mandir (Red Temple, Chandni Chowk), Old Delhi (Shahjahanabad), District Central Delhi, Delhi - 470001
description: Shri Digambar Jain Lal Mandir (Red Temple, Chandni Chowk) is an auspicious Digambar Jain pilgrimage destination situated in Old Delhi (Shahjahanabad), Delhi. The oldest and best-known Digambar Jain temple in Delhi, situated directly opposite the Red Fort at the entrance to Netaji Subhash Marg and Chandni Chowk. Established in 1656 CE during the reign of Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan, it originated as the 'Urdu Mandir' (Camp Temple) for Jain military officers and imperial merchants. Built in striking red sandstone, the complex houses ancient Jinabimbas dating from the 10th–15th centuries and the renowned Charity Birds Hospital (Jain Chidiya Aspatal) established in 1956.
history: When Emperor Shah Jahan shifted the Mughal capital from Agra to Shahjahanabad (Delhi) in 1648, a contingent of Jain cavalry officers and royal treasurers was granted land to establish their camp opposite the imperial citadel. In 1656, an imperial officer installed a sacred image of Lord Parshvanatha in a tent sanctuary, which gradually expanded into a permanent red sandstone structure known as the Urdu Mandir. During the later Mughal period, sacred metal and stone Tirthankara idols from ancient temples in Mewar and Gwalior were brought here for preservation. In 1800–1807, Raja Harsukh Rai and community leaders renovated the sanctum, and in the early 20th century, the imposing red sandstone shikhara was added. Carr Stephen (1876) notes the prominent commercial and spiritual status of the Digambar merchant community surrounding Chandni Chowk.
religious_significance: Premier spiritual and institutional landmark of the Digambar Jain community in northern India, receiving hundreds of thousands of pilgrims annually.
moolnayak_details: Bhagwan Rishabhanatha (Adinath), in contemplative Padmasana (Seated) posture, measuring approximately 3 feet, sculpted from Black Kasauti Stone, dating to the Medieval (c. 11th–12th Century CE), (Ancient seated Vitaraga idol with bull lanchhana, accompanied by historical brass idols of Parshvanatha and Chandraprabhu.).

darshan_timings.notes: Temple opens early for morning pakhsal; visitors are requested to wear traditional clean clothes.

name: Shri Digambar Jain Naya Mandir (Dharampura, Chandni Chowk)
hindi_name: श्री दिगंबर जैन नया मंदिर (धर्मपुरा, चाँदनी चौक)
address: Shri Digambar Jain Naya Mandir (Dharampura, Chandni Chowk), Old Delhi (Dharampura), District Central Delhi, Delhi - 454001
description: Shri Digambar Jain Naya Mandir (Dharampura, Chandni Chowk) is an auspicious Digambar Jain pilgrimage destination situated in Old Delhi (Dharampura), Delhi. A monumental Digambar Jain temple in Dharampura, Old Delhi, constructed in 1807 CE (VS 1864) by Raja Harsukh Rai, royal treasurer to Mughal Emperor Akbar II. Revered as the first Jain temple in the Mughal imperial capital to be granted an official imperial firman permitting the erection of stone shikharas (spires), which had been prohibited in Delhi for centuries. The temple houses an extraordinary subterranean Jnana Bhandar preserving priceless medieval Digambar manuscripts.
history: Raja Harsukh Rai, an influential Agarwala Digambar Jain merchant and imperial treasurer, secured a special royal decree (firman) from Mughal Emperor Akbar II allowing the construction of soaring stone shikharas in the walled city of Shahjahanabad. The grand consecration ceremony (Panchakalyanaka Pratishtha) in 1807 was celebrated with unprecedented splendor, attended by Digambar sanghas from across northern and western India. Raja Harsukh Rai also established a subterranean Jnana Bhandar (scriptural repository) to safeguard rare palm-leaf and handmade paper manuscripts, including illuminated texts of the Samayasara and Uttarapurana with gold calligraphy.
religious_significance: Renowned for its architectural magnificence, imperial historical significance, and one of northern India's richest private collections of Digambar Jain manuscripts (Jnana Bhandar).
moolnayak_details: Bhagwan Parshvanatha, in contemplative Padmasana (Seated) posture, measuring approximately 3.5 feet, sculpted from White Makrana Marble, dating to the 1807 CE (Constituted with ancient Pratimas), (Exquisitely polished marble image with seven-hooded serpent canopy (Dharanendra nagafana) and attendant Yaksha-Yakshi carvings.).

name: Shri Shatrunjaya Tirth (Palitana)
address: Shatrunjaya Hill, Palitana, Bhavnagar District, Gujarat - 364270
description: The world-famous city of over 860 white marble temples perched atop the Shatrunjaya hills, consecrated to the first Tirthankara, Bhagwan Rishabhdev (Adinath).
history: Visited countlessly by the first Tirthankara Rishabhdev. Pundarika Swami, the chief Gandhara of Rishabhdev, attained liberation here with millions of Munis. The present temple complex was renovated across dynasties from the 11th to 16th century CE.
religious_significance: Considered the eternal pilgrimage (Sasvata Tirth). Over 860 marble temples adorn the two summits and the saddle joining them, making it one of the largest temple complexes in the world.
moolnayak_details: Bhagwan Rishabhdev (Adinath) in Padmasana posture with radiant jeweled eyes inside the main sanctum (Chaumukha and Adishwar temples).

darshan_timings.aarti: Pakhsal at sunrise, Sandhya Aarti at dusk
darshan_timings.notes: Nobody is permitted to stay overnight on the sacred hill; devotees must descend before nightfall.
darshan_timings.morning: 6:30 AM - 1:00 PM (Hill ascent opens around 5:30 AM)

accessibility_notes: About 3,750 stone-carved steps to the summit. Doli (chair carriers) are available for elderly pilgrims.

nearby_transport.road: Direct state transport and private buses from Ahmedabad, Surat, and Mumbai
nearby_transport.airport: Bhavnagar Airport (BHU) - 55 km / Ahmedabad Airport (AMD) - 215 km
nearby_transport.railway: Palitana Railway Station (PIT) - 4 km / Bhavnagar Terminus (BVC) - 50 km

name: Shri Shravanabelagola Tirth
address: Vindhyagiri Hill, Shravanabelagola, Hassan District, Karnataka - 573135
description: Home to the world's tallest monolithic stone statue, the 57-foot Bhagwan Bahubali (Gommateshwara), carved in 981 CE by Ganga dynasty general Chavundaraya.
history: Consecrated on 13 March 981 CE. Chandragupta Maurya and Acharya Bhadrabahu stayed and attained Sallekhana on the opposite Chandragiri hill in the 3rd century BCE, making it one of the oldest living Jain learning seats.
religious_significance: The Mahamastakabhisheka ceremony celebrated every 12 years draws hundreds of thousands of pilgrims from across the globe. Features over 800 rock inscriptions spanning a millennium.
moolnayak_details: Bhagwan Bahubali (Gommateshwara) — 57-foot single granite monolith in Kayotsarga posture depicting profound equanimity with creepers entwined around limbs.

darshan_timings.aarti: 7:00 AM (Mahamastakabhisheka daily ritual) and 6:00 PM
darshan_timings.notes: Steps can get warm during sunny afternoons; morning or late afternoon ascent is recommended.

accessibility_notes: 650 carved stone steps climb up Vindhyagiri Hill. Hand-carried palanquin (doli) service is available.

nearby_transport.road: Well connected via NH-75 from Bengaluru (145 km) and Mysuru (85 km)
nearby_transport.airport: Bengaluru International Airport (BLR) - 165 km

name: Sihoniya Shantinatha Digambar Atishaya Kshetra
address: Sihoniya Shantinatha Digambar Atishaya Kshetra, Sihoniya, District Morena, Madhya Pradesh - 476001
description: Sihoniya Shantinatha Digambar Atishaya Kshetra is an auspicious Digambar Jain pilgrimage destination situated in Sihoniya, Madhya Pradesh. The ancient capital of the Kachchhapaghata dynasty (11th century CE), famous for its monumental 15-foot high seated monolithic sandstone idol of Lord Shantinatha. Detailed in Chapter 13 of Dr. Kailash Chand Jain's treatise as one of northern Madhya Pradesh's supreme medieval sculpting achievements.
history: Founded as the political seat of the Kachchhapaghata ruler Kirtiraja and his successors in the 11th century CE. An inscription dated Samvat 1072 records the consecration of the great Shantinatha idol by merchant leaders under Digambar monastic guidance. Surrounding fields continue to yield ornate Tirthankara bronzes, pillars, and inscriptions.
religious_significance: Revered as an miraculous Atishaya Kshetra where prayers for peace and liberation are answered.
moolnayak_details: Bhagwan Shantinatha, in contemplative Padmasana (Seated) posture, measuring approximately 15 feet (4.5 meters), sculpted from Red Sandstone, dating to the 1015 CE (Samvat 1072), (Deer cognizance (lanchhana) inscribed on the lotus throne; flanked by Indra and celestial attendants.).

description: Tirumalai Neminatha Cave & Hill Complex is an auspicious Digambar Jain pilgrimage destination situated in Polur, Tamil Nadu. A monumental ancient hill sanctuary in northern Tamil Nadu, housing three rock-cut cave temples, an active structural temple, medieval Chola murals, and a celebrated 16-foot monolithic rock-relief idol of Lord Neminatha (the tallest Jain sculpture in Tamil Nadu). Detailed in Chapter 13 of Dr. Kailash Chand Jain's treatise.
history: Inhabited by Digambar ascetics from the early centuries CE. Chola queen Kundavai (sister of Rajaraja Chola I) and Sambuvaraya chieftains granted substantial endowments between the 10th and 14th centuries, recorded in numerous Tamil inscriptions on the cliff faces.
religious_significance: Foremost active Digambar Jain archaeological sanctuary in Tamil Nadu.
moolnayak_details: Bhagwan Neminatha Monolith, in contemplative Khadgasana (Standing) posture, measuring approximately 16 feet (4.87 meters), sculpted from Granite Cliff Relief, dating to the 10th–11th Century CE, (Standing in Kayotsarga with conch symbol and celestial fly-whisk attendants.).
